'''''Venegasia''''' is a genus of [[North America]]n plants in the tribe [[Madieae]] within the family [[Asteraceae]].<ref>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/149984#page/48/mode/1up Candolle, Augustin Pyramus de. 1838.  Prodromus Systematis Naturalis Regni Vegetabilis 6: 43] in Latin</ref><ref name=i>[http://www.tropicos.org/Name/40023655 Tropicos, ''Venegasia'' DC.]</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=134457 Flora of North America, Vol. 21 Page 385 ''Venegasia'' de Candolle ]</ref><ref>Turner, B. L. and D. Zippin. 1992. Taxonomic study of ''Venegasia'' (Asteraceae: Helenieae). Sida 15: 223–229</ref>

'''''Venegasia carpesioides''''' is the only known species in the genus. It is shrubby bush growing to 1.8 m tall and prefers locations in moist canyons in southern [[California]],<ref>[http://www.calflora.net/bloomingplants/canyonsunflower.html Calflora, University of California @ Berkeley, Canyon sunflower]</ref> and in [[Baja California]]. It is commonly known as the '''canyon sunflower.'''<ref name=g>[http://dixon.iplantcollaborative.org/CompositaeWeb/Default.aspx?Page=NameSearch&searchText=Venegasia Flann, C (ed) 2009+ Global Compositae Checklist ]{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Venegasia%20carpesioides.png Biota of North America Program 2013 county distribution map]</ref>

''Venegasia'' was named after the [[Mexican people|Mexican]] historian [[Miguel Venegas]], 1680–1764.<ref>[http://www.calflora.net/botanicalnames/pageV.html CalFlora Botanical Names]</ref>
